whatChanged.title: Past English is working across more kinds of communication
whatChanged.summary: Across six attended lessons, Gustavo has used past-time English to talk about his own experiences, answer and ask questions, retell information and repair several present/past mismatches. On 29 September, this appeared across personal speaking, short answers, questions and a short retell. Some forms were produced without a direct language model and others became more accurate after a clue. The clearest precision priority remains did/didn't + base verb.
whatChanged.evidence: Lessons 1–6 show recurring past-language use in meaningful contexts. Lesson 5 included “I don't” → “No, I didn't”. Lesson 6 added learner-generated forms such as “I played volleyball...”, “Did you go to the mall?”, “Yes, I did”, “I ate...”, “Where did you go?”, “Did you play?” and “He ate barbecue and ice cream”, alongside both self-initiated and cue-supported repair. “I didn't went to school” remains direct evidence that did/didn't + base verb is not yet consistent.

priorities.title: Tell real stories about the past
priorities.why: Past English is already appearing in meaningful communication. The next step is making that language more reliable across a complete story without interrupting the first attempt.
priorities.evidence: Across the six lessons, Gustavo has used past forms to talk about trips, school, food and other parts of his own life. Lesson 6 broadened this to statements, questions, short answers and retelling.

priorities.title: Notice NOW vs PAST while speaking
priorities.why: Gustavo can often recover the correct time form and has shown real self-monitoring. More spontaneous mixed present/past questions will help that noticing become more consistent.
priorities.evidence: Lesson 5 showed the self-correction “I don't” → “No, I didn't”. Lesson 6 added several repairs, including Do→Did and go→went patterns, with a mix of self-initiated and cue-supported correction.

priorities.title: Make did / didn't + base verb more automatic
priorities.why: This is now a precise form-level priority inside an otherwise increasingly productive past-time system.
priorities.evidence: Gustavo can recover the base-form rule in several tasks, but “I didn't went to school” still appeared on 29 September.

nextAction.outcome: Prepare Gustavo for the upcoming school-English assessment while preserving a short first-attempt window to observe how past-time language and self-correction now work with less interruption.

nextAction.evidence: The learner self-check-in is already persisted. Lesson 6 broadened past-time use across statements, questions, short answers, retelling and repair, while the school assessment was identified as the immediate practical priority.

classReports.teacherInsight: Primary transcript evidence shows successful supported retrieval. Gustavo repeated 'give us energy' for carbohydrates, classified foods, reconstructed the digestive route and correctly retrieved the large intestine as the site of water absorption. The lesson supports consolidation, not a claim of independent mastery of every item.

classReports.title: Class Report - 15 Sep 2026
classReports.summary: Returned to general English after the Science review. Gustavo checked Science memory after one week, contrasted Do/Did answers, reused past verbs and built personal sentences.
classReports.teacherInsight: Transfer points — Evidence: After “Did you go...?”, Gustavo first answered “I don't” and then changed it to “No, I didn't”. He also reused went and drank in personal sentences and recalled part of the Science language after one week. Interpretation: Past meaning is returning across contexts and there is emerging evidence of self-monitoring while speaking. Boundary: One self-correction does not establish mastery, and Science recall varied between independent retrieval and reconstruction with support. Next verification: Invite a new real past story, contrast Do/Did, let Gustavo attempt retrieval before help, and use a short learner-awareness check-in.

classReports.title: Class Report - 29 Sep 2026
classReports.summary: Gustavo used past-time English across personal statements, short answers, questions and a short retelling. Several forms were produced without a direct language model, while other present/past forms became more accurate after a clue. did/didn't + base verb remained inconsistent, making it a precise next priority rather than evidence that Past Simple is unavailable.
classReports.teacherInsight: Transfer points — Evidence: Gustavo used past language across several communicative functions, including “I played volleyball...”, “Did you go to the mall?”, “Yes, I did”, “I ate...”, “Where did you go?”, “Did you play?” and “He ate barbecue and ice cream”. He also showed both self-initiated and cue-supported repair. Interpretation: Past-time language is increasingly usable in communication, and self-monitoring is becoming a genuine longitudinal pattern. Boundary: reliability still varies by form and condition; “I didn't went to school” shows that did/didn't + base verb remains an active precision priority. Next verification: Begin with one uninterrupted personal past story, record autonomous versus cue-supported repair separately, then move into the upcoming school-English assessment revision.

grammarOverview.title: Language We Are Building
grammarOverview.summary: The aim is not to collect grammar labels. These language patterns matter because they help Gustavo tell stories, understand time, give advice, describe relationships between actions and people, compare things, and use English to learn.
focusPoints: Talking about past experiences: use forms such as went and drank, and didn't + base verb.
Understanding time in questions: Do...? usually asks about routines or the present; Did...? asks about completed past events.
Giving advice: use should / shouldn't to say what someone could do.
Actions that return to the same person: myself, yourself, himself, herself.
Comparing one thing with all the others: shorter words often use -est; longer words often use the most; some forms are irregular, such as best.
Science in English: useful academic vocabulary and sequencing remain available for reuse when relevant.

teacherFeedback.title: Your first six-lesson journey
teacherFeedback.body: Across these six lessons, Gustavo has been using English increasingly to talk about things that belong to his own world — holidays, school, sports, games and experiences. Past language has returned repeatedly in meaningful contexts. On 15 September there was a clear self-correction; on 29 September he used Simple Past in affirmative answers, short answers, questions and a short retell, and repaired several present/past forms after a cue. English has also continued to work as a tool for school content. The important story is not simply what was right or wrong: it is that Gustavo is using, revisiting, noticing and reconnecting language over time while some forms, especially did/didn't + base verb, still need consolidation.

teacherFeedback.title: Leitura pedagógica da jornada
teacherFeedback.body: Aprender não acontece em linha reta. Uma aula pode apresentar algo novo, fortalecer algo antigo, revelar um erro útil, recuperar uma ideia depois de alguns dias ou ajudar o aluno a perceber melhor o próprio inglês. O próximo ciclo vai preservar essa lógica: cada aula terá uma direção, sem exigir uma 'mudança de estado' artificial. Queremos que Gustavo se torne também um observador da própria aprendizagem — percebendo o que já consegue fazer, o que consegue tentar com ajuda e o que ainda quer estudar mais.

cumulativeImpact.title: Learning Journey — First 6 Lessons
cumulativeImpact.summary: Across six attended lessons, Gustavo has moved from reactivating English through personal conversation to using past-time language across a wider range of real functions: telling, answering, questioning, retelling and repairing. He has also used English to work with school content. The important story is not one isolated verb or one correction: it is that past meaning is becoming increasingly usable while some precision, especially did/didn't + base verb, is still becoming reliable.
evidence: 6 attended lessons confirmed: 18 Aug, 25 Aug, 01 Sep, 08 Sep, 15 Sep and 29 Sep 2026.
Past meaning returned repeatedly across personal conversation, school review and follow-up tasks rather than appearing only once.
15 Sep: self-correction from “I don't” to “No, I didn't” after a past question.

29 Sep: past English appeared across personal statements, questions, short answers and retelling, including “I played volleyball...”, “Did you go to the mall?”, “Yes, I did”, “I ate...”, “Where did you go?” and “He ate barbecue and ice cream”.
29 Sep: both self-initiated and cue-supported repair were observed; “I didn't went to school” still showed that did/didn't + base verb needs consolidation.
The learner self-check-in is already persisted as learner self-perception evidence and is not treated as a proficiency score.
No CEFR level movement beyond teacher-confirmed CEFR A1 is claimed from these six lessons.
